summary: In low-power networks, memory-constrained routers may only hold a few routes. This RFC defines an IPv6 routing header carrying a source route, so packets can be delivered when RPL stores most routes at a root node.

plainLanguage.summary: Some routers in a low-power network have memory for only a few default routes, so they cannot store a map of every destination. This document gives them a way to pass a packet on anyway: the packet carries the list of routers to visit. Each router reads the next address from the list and forwards the packet there.

questions: source routes in low power networks
what is the rpl source routing header
subtitle: An IPv6 header that names every hop in the packet, so tiny low-power routers need no routing table.

tldr.problem: Routers in low-power and lossy networks may have memory for only a few default routes, yet they still have to pass packets to any destination inside the network.
tldr.mechanism: A new IPv6 Routing header type, the Source Routing Header (Routing Type 3), lists every hop of the path inside the packet. A router forwards by reading the next address from the header instead of looking up a route.
tldr.outcome: The header can compress addresses that share a prefix, and strict rules limit where it may be used, which answers the problems that led to the Type 0 Routing header being deprecated.

facts.label: Address entry size
facts.value: 16 - CmprI octets, and 16 - CmprE for the last entry

facts.label: Reserved field
facts.value: Initialised to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver

today: RFC 6554 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used with RFC 6550, which defines RPL itself.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) is a distance vector IPv6 routing protocol designed for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs), networks constrained in communication data rate, processing power, energy capacity and memory. Some LLN configurations use routers whose memory limits allow them to keep only a small number of default routes and no other destinations. Those routers still have to forward datagrams and keep reachability to destinations inside the network.

To use paths that include those memory-constrained routers, RPL relies on source routing. In one deployment model of RPL, more capable routers collect routing information and form paths to arbitrary destinations within a routing domain. A source routing mechanism supported by IPv6 is then needed to deliver the datagrams.

This document specifies the Source Routing Header (SRH) for use strictly between RPL routers in the same RPL routing domain, which is a collection of RPL routers under the control of a single administration. The boundaries of routing domains are set by network management, which marks some links as exterior, or inter-domain, links.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routers in a sensor network cannot keep a list of every destination. The packet carries that list instead, so a router only has to read the next address and forward the packet.

sections.title: Two Ways to Carry a Source Route
sections.content:
The format of the SRH is drawn from the Type 0 Routing header (RH0) of RFC 2460, with two changes. First, the SRH adds fields that let the source route entries be compressed when all of them share a prefix with the IPv6 Destination Address of the packet carrying it, which is a common situation in an LLN. Compression saves scarce resources such as channel capacity. Second, the SRH changes the processing rules to answer the security concerns that led to RH0 being deprecated in RFC 5095.

Those processing rules are three. RPL routers implement a strict source route policy, so every IPv6 hop between the source and the destination of the source route is named in the SRH. An SRH is used only between RPL routers within one routing domain, and RPL Border Routers, which connect routing domains and IP domains that use other routing protocols, do not let a datagram carrying an SRH enter or exit a routing domain. A RPL router also drops any datagram that includes more than one address assigned to any of its own interfaces, which avoids forwarding loops.

Two cases determine how an SRH is included. If the SRH specifies the complete path from source to destination, the router places the SRH directly in the datagram. If the SRH specifies only part of the path, the router uses IPv6-in-IPv6 tunnelling, as defined in RFC 2473, and places the SRH in the outer IPv6 header. Tunnelling ensures the datagram is delivered unmodified and that ICMP errors return to the source of the SRH rather than to the source of the original datagram.

Case 1 applies when both source and destination are inside the routing domain and one SRH names the whole path. The source address sits in the IPv6 header's Source Address field, and the destination address sits in the last SRH entry for all but the last hop; for the last hop it is in the IPv6 header's Destination Address field. Case 2 applies to every datagram whose source or destination lies outside the routing domain, and also whenever a RPL router inserts a source route while forwarding a datagram. The outer header, including the SRH, is added and removed by the RPL router.
sections.plainLanguage: The header lists every router the packet must visit. If the list covers the whole path, the header sits inside the packet. If it covers only part of the path, the router wraps the packet in another IPv6 header and puts the list there.

sections.title: The Source Routing Header Format
sections.content:
The SRH begins with four 8-bit fields. Next Header names the type of the header that follows and uses the same values as the IPv6 Next Header field. Hdr Ext Len is the length of the Routing header in 8-octet units, not counting the first 8 octets; when the addresses are compressed, it does not equal twice the number of addresses. Routing Type identifies the particular variant, and an SRH sets it to 3. Segments Left is the number of route segments remaining, that is, the number of explicitly listed intermediate nodes still to be visited before the final destination, and the originator sets it to n, the number of addresses in Addresses[1..n].

The next row holds CmprI and CmprE, each 4 bits, plus Pad, also 4 bits, and a Reserved field. CmprI is the number of prefix octets elided from every segment except the last, so the entries 1 to n-1 each occupy 16 minus CmprI octets. CmprE is the number of prefix octets elided from the last segment, which occupies 16 minus CmprE octets. Pad is the number of octets used for padding after Address[n]. The sender MUST initialise Reserved to zero and the receiver MUST ignore it.

The address vector follows. The originator places the next hop's IPv6 address in the IPv6 header's Destination Address field and the second hop's address as the first entry, Address[1]. Because a common configuration is that all routers in a routing domain share a prefix, CmprI and CmprE say how many leading octets of each address are the same as the IPv6 Destination Address of the packet carrying the SRH, and those octets are not repeated in the header. When CmprI and CmprE are both 0, Pad MUST be 0.

An SRH MUST NOT specify a path that visits a node more than once. The source may not know the mapping between IPv6 addresses and nodes, so it MUST at least ensure that no IPv6 address appears more than once and that the Source and Destination addresses of the encapsulating datagram do not appear in the SRH. Multicast addresses MUST NOT appear in an SRH or in the IPv6 Destination Address field of a datagram carrying an SRH.
sections.plainLanguage: The header carries a list of addresses. Two fields say how many leading bytes of each address can be left out when they match the packet's destination address, and that shortens the list.

sections.title: Generating Source Routing Headers
sections.content:
To deliver an IPv6 datagram to its destination, a router may need to generate a new SRH and specify a strict source route. When the router is the source of the original packet and the destination is known to be within the same RPL routing domain, the router SHOULD include the SRH directly within the original packet. Otherwise the router MUST use IPv6-in-IPv6 tunnelling and place the SRH in the tunnel header, so that the delivered datagram stays unmodified and ICMPv6 errors are sent back to the router that generated the SRH.

When tunnelling, and in order to respect the IPv6 Hop Limit value of the original datagram, a RPL router generating an SRH MUST set Segments Left to less than the original datagram's IPv6 Hop Limit value upon forwarding. If the source route is longer than the original Hop Limit, only the initial hops, as many as the Hop Limit allows, go into the SRH. If the RPL router is not the source of the original datagram, the original datagram's Hop Limit field is decremented before the SRH is generated. After generating the SRH, the RPL router decrements the original datagram's Hop Limit value by the SRH Segments Left value. Handling both fields this way means ICMPv6 Time Exceeded errors occur as they would on a more traditional IPv6 network that forwards datagrams without tunnelling.

To avoid fragmentation, it is desirable to employ MTU sizes that allow for the header expansion, that is, at least 1280 plus 40 for the outer IP header plus SRH_MAX_SIZE, where SRH_MAX_SIZE is the maximum path length for a given RPL network. For that to work the communicating endpoints need to know the MTU along the path, for example through Path MTU Discovery. The larger MTU size may not be available on all links, such as the 1280 octets on IPv6 Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) links. Much of the traffic on these networks is expected to consist of much smaller messages than the MTU, so performance degradation through fragmentation should be limited.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router builds the list, it must not exceed the packet's hop limit, which counts how many routers the packet may pass through. It lowers the hop limit by the number of hops it listed, so that error messages still come out at the right point.

sections.title: Processing Source Routing Headers
sections.content:
As specified in RFC 2460, a routing header is not examined or processed until it reaches the node identified in the Destination Address field of the IPv6 header. In that node, dispatching on the Next Header field of the immediately preceding header causes the Routing header module to be invoked.

After the routing header has been processed and the IPv6 datagram resubmitted to the IPv6 module, the IPv6 Destination Address holds the next hop's address. When forwarding a datagram that contains an SRH with a non-zero Segments Left value, if the IPv6 Destination Address is not on-link, a router MUST drop the datagram and SHOULD send an ICMP Destination Unreachable message (ICMPv6 Type 1) with ICMPv6 Code set to 7 to the packet's Source Address. That code means the IPv6 Destination Address is not on-link and the router cannot satisfy the strict source route requirement. The rules in Section 2.4 of RFC 4443 apply when generating those error messages.

To detect loops in the SRH, a router MUST determine whether the SRH includes multiple addresses assigned to any interface on that router. If such addresses appear more than once and are separated by at least one address not assigned to that router, the router MUST drop the packet and SHOULD send an ICMP Parameter Problem, Code 0, to the Source Address. This loop check adds significant per-packet processing overhead, but it is required to mitigate the bandwidth exhaustion attacks that led to RH0 being deprecated.

The processing algorithm is set out in the RFC. If Segments Left is 0, the router proceeds to process the next header, whose type is identified by the Next Header field in the Routing header. Otherwise the router computes n, the number of addresses in the Routing header, and checks that Segments Left is not greater than n, in which case it sends an ICMP Parameter Problem, Code 0, pointing to the Segments Left field, and discards the packet. It then decrements Segments Left by one and computes i, the index of the next address to be visited, by subtracting Segments Left from n. If Address[i] or the IPv6 Destination Address is multicast, the packet is discarded. If two or more entries in Address[1..n] are assigned to a local interface and are separated by at least one address not assigned to that interface, the router sends an ICMP Parameter Problem (Code 0) and discards the packet. Otherwise it swaps the IPv6 Destination Address and Address[i], checks that the IPv6 Hop Limit is greater than 1, decrements the Hop Limit by one, and resubmits the packet to the IPv6 module for transmission to the new destination.

RPL routers are responsible for ensuring that an SRH is only used between RPL routers. A datagram destined to a RPL router is processed in the usual way; if the SRH was included in tunnelled mode and the RPL router serves as the tunnel endpoint, the router removes the outer IPv6 header, and with it the SRH. A datagram destined elsewhere within the same routing domain is forwarded to the correct interface. A datagram destined outside the routing domain is dropped if the outermost IPv6 header contains an SRH that was not generated by the RPL router forwarding it.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that receives the list checks three things: that the next address is on the same link, that the list does not send the packet back to the router twice, and that the list holds no group address. It then swaps the next address into the packet's destination field and forwards the packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RPL message security mechanisms defined in RFC 6550 do not apply to the Source Routing Header. This specification does not provide any confidentiality, integrity or authenticity mechanism to protect the SRH.

RFC 5095 deprecates the Type 0 Routing header because of the significant attacks it lists: bypassing filtering devices, reaching otherwise unreachable Internet systems, network topology discovery, bandwidth exhaustion, and defeating anycast. Because the SRH is only for use within a RPL routing domain, such attacks cannot be mounted from outside a routing domain. RPL routers MUST drop datagrams entering or exiting a routing domain that contain an SRH in the IPv6 extension headers.

The attacks can still be mounted from inside a routing domain. To mitigate bandwidth exhaustion attacks, this specification requires RPL routers to check for loops in the SRH and drop datagrams that contain such loops. Attacks that bypass filtering devices or reach otherwise unreachable systems are not as relevant in mesh networks, whose topologies are by their very nature highly dynamic. The RPL routing protocol is designed to provide reachability to all devices within a routing domain and may use routes that traverse any number of devices in any order. Even so, these attacks and others, such as defeating anycast and routing topology discovery, can occur within a routing domain when using this specification.

The generation of ICMPv6 error messages may be used to attempt denial-of-service attacks, by sending an error-causing SRH in back-to-back datagrams. An implementation that correctly follows Section 2.4 of RFC 4443 would be protected by the ICMPv6 rate-limiting mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of hops travels in the clear and is not protected in any way. It is only allowed inside one routing domain, and routers drop datagrams that carry it across a domain boundary. Inside the domain, a router still checks the list for loops, so a packet cannot be made to circle and consume bandwidth.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: This document defines a new IPv6 Routing Type, the RPL Source Route Header, which has been assigned number 3 by IANA. It also defines a new ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable Code, Error in Source Routing Header, which has been assigned number 7 by IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA gave this header the routing type number 3 and the new error code the number 7.

viz.caption: THE RPL SOURCE ROUTING HEADER (RFC 6554, SECTION 3)

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Identifies the type of header immediately following the Routing header. Uses the same values as the IPv6 Next Header field.

fields.name: Hdr Ext Len
fields.desc: Length of the Routing header in 8-octet units, not including the first 8 octets.

fields.name: Routing Type
fields.desc: Identifies the particular Routing header variant. An SRH sets this to 3.

fields.name: Segments Left
fields.desc: Number of route segments remaining, that is, intermediate nodes still to be visited before the final destination.

fields.name: CmprI
fields.desc: Number of prefix octets elided from each segment except the last. Each entry 1 to n-1 is then 16 minus CmprI octets.

fields.name: CmprE
fields.desc: Number of prefix octets elided from the last segment, which is then 16 minus CmprE octets.

fields.name: Pad
fields.desc: Number of octets used for padding after Address[n]. Must be 0 when CmprI and CmprE are both 0.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Unused. The sender MUST initialise it to zero and the receiver MUST ignore it.

fields.name: Addresses[1..n]
fields.desc: Vector of addresses numbered 1 to n. The next hop sits in the IPv6 Destination Address field and the second hop is Address[1].

viz.caption: THE TWO CASES FOR CARRYING A SOURCE ROUTE (RFC 6554, SECTION 2)

cells: In the outer IPv6 header of an IPv6-in-IPv6 tunnel
The SRH names the complete path from source to destination
The SRH names only part of the path, or the source or destination is outside the routing domain
The RPL router, which also removes it at the far end

viz.caption: THE THREE RULES THAT KEEP THE HEADER SAFE (RFC 6554, SECTION 2)

items.title: Strict source route
items.text: Every IPv6 hop between the source and the destination of the source route is named in the SRH.

items.title: One routing domain only
items.text: RPL Border Routers do not let a datagram carrying an SRH enter or exit a RPL routing domain.

items.title: Loop check
items.text: A router drops datagrams that include more than one address assigned to any of its own interfaces.
